body:
The issue over the heredibility of IQ and intelligence is likely to drag on
'till the end of time.  I think it's important that people, both
hereditarians and those who emphasize environmental influences, try to be as
objective as possible with the issue.  Unfortunately, emotions have been
tied to discussions related to IQ its heredibility.  Even worse, many,
particularly in the scientific community, have deemphasized the implications
of IQ.  They have ignored compelling quantative data that has shown that
g -- or general intelligence -- is more than a mere creation of the
mathematical machinations of factor analysis.  They have ignored the fact
that IQ is, albeit with limitations, the best predictor of academic
performance, and correlates highly with SES outcome.

Okay, as human beings we are more than mere numbers.  The brain is immensly
complicated, moreso than any computer chip that could ever be developed.
Moreover, the definition of intelligence itself is bound to carry some
subjectivity, depending on who you talk to about the subject.  Given the
fears of potential abuses that might emanate if groups are found, or proven,
to differ in intelligence, it's not surprising that there is so much concern
and obfuscation over the issue.  In fact, it might actually be good if
science is, at times, suppressed for the social "good" (I know this might
strike a chord in some right-wing readers.)  But, on the other hand, who is
to say what is the social good, and where should we draw the line as to what
type of scientific research should be prohibited, if any?

I think a part of the problem is that many, particularly among the
left-wing, have attached too much importance to intelligence (either
consciously or subconsciously.)  Otherwise, there wouldn't be such a fuss
over the IQ issue; there wouldn't be concerns that people might be "proven"
to be superior or inferior.  Ted Kaczynski wrote about this:

"This also underlies the rejection by many leftists of the concept of mental
illness and of the utility of IQ tests. Leftists are antagonistic to genetic
explanations of human abilities or behavior because such explanations tend
to make some persons appear superior or inferior to others. Leftists prefer
to give society the credit or blame for an individual's ability or lack of
it. Thus if a person is 'inferior' it is not his fault, but society's,
because he has not been brought up properly."

In any case, I think it should be emphasized that intragroup differences are
greater than intergroup differences, and that we should all should be viewed
equal in the context of law; not to mention, we should be given the same
opportunity for the pursuit of life, liberty and happiness.

;o)

Here are some interesting quotes:

"Nothing in 'The Bell Curve' angered me more than the authors' failure to
supply any justification for their central claim, the sine qua non of their
entire argument: that the number known as g, the celebrated 'general factor'
of intelligence ... captures a real property in the head."

--Stephen Jay Gould

"If modern neuroscience reveals biochemical differences that account for
human variability, we must deal with this important knowledge; ... ignoring
differences because they could become abuses will not make them go away."

--Candace Pert (Biochemist at the National Institute of Mental Health,
Reviewing Gould's Mismeasure of Man)

"Good intentions are impotent unless based on reality."

--Arthur R. Jensen (Educability and Group Differences)
